result: The authors developed a low-cost (<$1) side-view observation device using 3D-printed components and a first-surface mirror that enables simultaneous bottom- and side-view imaging of 3D spheroids on inverted microscopes. The device features magnetic connections for positioning adjustment and works effectively with 4×, 10×, and 20× objective lenses, though 40× imaging has limitations due to working distance constraints and chromatic aberration.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly praised the device design. One reviewer stated it is 'an ingenious design' and another called it 'a wonderful design to view the 3D cell spheroids.' The reviewers confirmed 'the authors provide compelling evidence that the methods work as described' and noted the system's compatibility with inverted microscopes and its low production cost.

result: The device was applied to track spheroid formation dynamics in situ, revealing that cells initially aggregate in a planar ring structure with negligible thickness changes, then gradually compact into a 3D spheroid as the x-y dimension decreases and height increases until the height-to-width ratio approaches 1. This represents the first time side-profile changes during spheroid formation have been depicted without disrupting the sample.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed this capability, noting the system 'allows the in situ observation of the 3D structures along the 3 axes (x,y and z) without disrupting the integrity of the spheroids' and enables 'follow[ing] in real-time tumour spheroid formation...without disrupting their integrity.' The time-lapse tracking capability was highlighted as allowing 'a better understanding of the cell aggregation/growth and kinetic of the cells.'

result: During migration assays, side-view observation revealed that cells migrate from the spheroid periphery while the inner width remains largely unchanged (6.8% decrease), the spheroid thickness decreases from 242 to 131 μm, and the contact angle increases from 0° to 172°. The dark core height ratio increased from 0.61 to 0.69, indicating that proliferating cells at the outer region are the prominent participants in migration.
evaluation: Reviewers specifically highlighted this finding, noting 'the system allows the analysis of cell migration/escape from the 3D structure analysing not only the morphological changes in the periphery of the spheroids but also from the inner region demonstrating that the proliferating cells in the periphery of the structure are more involved in the migration and dissemination process.' This was identified as a key strength of the method.

result: Side-view imaging revealed that dark core formation timing is inversely related to seeding density, but the z-direction height at dark core onset remains consistent at approximately 250 ± 15 μm across all seeding densities. This suggests a critical threshold of ~250 μm for effective oxygen diffusion, aligning with previous findings of a 500 μm maximum viable diameter.
evaluation: Reviewers did not explicitly critique this finding and accepted the correlation between spheroid thickness and dark core formation. The observation was presented as enabled by the side-view device, which reviewers confirmed 'work[s] as described' and provides 'more comprehensive information than the traditional one angle of imaging.'

result: Side-view observation of spheroid fusion revealed that two spheroids form symmetric necks that gradually fuse, with the contact length progressively approaching the z-direction thickness and the contact angle reaching 171° after 100 hr. Conventional bottom-view imaging alone would miss critical structural changes on the opposite side of the fusion process.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the fusion tracking capability, noting the system enables 'follow[ing]...the spheroids fusion from multiple angles, allowing a better understanding of the cell aggregation/growth and kinetic of the cells.' The ability to observe from multiple angles was identified as a key advantage that provides 'more comprehensive information than the traditional one angle of imaging.'

result: DOX treatment caused surface roughness and dark core enlargement but did not significantly alter 3D morphology (only 0.64-2.24% change in height-to-width ratio), suggesting DOX induces cell death without disrupting overall spheroid structure. This contrasts with the distinct morphological features produced by different antitumor mechanisms.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly noted 'the application of the system in the study of the effects of doxorubicin and NK cells would give new insights in the description of the response of tumor 3D structure to killing agents.' The distinct outcomes between DOX and NK cell treatments were accepted as demonstrating the device's utility for drug testing applications.

result: NK-92 cell co-culture resulted in dramatic structural changes with the height-to-width ratio decreasing 37% (from 0.98 to 0.61) as NK cells gathered around, infiltrated, and gradually demolished the spheroid's 3D structure through membrane disruption and cell lysis. Side-view observation revealed four optically distinct regions at 16 hr and progressive collapse by 64 hr.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed this application, stating 'the application of the system in the study of the effects of doxorubicin and NK cells would give new insights in the description of the response of tumor 3D structure to killing agents.' The ability to track these structural changes was identified as a key strength demonstrating the device's utility.

result: Background claims establishing that 3D spheroids better recapitulate tumor microenvironments than 2D cultures, exhibit characteristic growth patterns and dark cores, and face imaging challenges with existing techniques including confocal microscopy, OCT, and LSFM due to light scattering and lack of standardized protocols.
evaluation: These are background/literature review claims supported by citations. Reviewers did not challenge these foundational statements and accepted the motivation for developing the new imaging device. The reviewers' positive reception of the device implicitly validates the stated limitations of existing approaches.

result: The correlation between spheroid thickness and dark core appearance was studied, with the dark core representing necrotic/quiescent zones from limited oxygen/nutrient diffusion, and light penetration being hindered by spheroid thickness, cellular layers, and extracellular matrix.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these biological and optical principles underlying the dark core observations. The acceptance of the dark core formation results (C60-C67) implicitly supports these mechanistic explanations. These claims provide context for interpreting the experimental findings.

result: Technical optimization results showing that spheroids were cultivated in agarose micro-wells, optimal imaging conditions included 90° lamp angle and 15 cm distance, and the device can image both single and multiple spheroids. Light absorption by agarose and DMEM medium causes magenta appearance.
evaluation: Reviewers confirmed 'the authors provide compelling evidence that the methods work as described,' which encompasses these technical details. No concerns were raised about the experimental setup or optimization parameters. These are accepted as supporting methodological details.

result: Contextual claims about previous limitations (requiring spheroid fixation for side-view), the biological importance of cell migration and fusion, and the use of spheroids for drug testing, with past studies assuming symmetrical geometries.
evaluation: These background claims supported by citations were not challenged by reviewers. They provide context for the novelty and significance of the new device. Reviewers' emphasis on the device enabling 'in situ' and 'real-time' observation implicitly validates the stated limitations of previous approaches.
